title: Lawsuit Challenges Trump's Tariffs on Canadian Goods
summary:
A lawsuit filed Tuesday in the U.S. Court of International Trade challenges President Donald Trump's tariffs on goods from Canada. A tariff is a tax on products brought in from another country.

The case was filed by the Liberty Justice Center, a nonprofit group, for Gellert Global Group, an American company that imports food. The lawsuit argues that Trump went beyond his powers as president by using a trade law from 1930 called Section 338.

Trump used Section 338 to put a 50% tax on many Canadian goods after trade talks broke down in August. The next month, the same law was used to ban some other Canadian products, including motorcycles and some alcohol and dairy products.

The White House says Section 338 lets the president add tariffs when a country treats U.S. sellers unfairly compared with sellers from other countries, even though the law has never been used that way before. A Trump administration official said the president's actions will be strongly defended in court.

The lawsuit says Canada's policies do not justify such large tariffs. It points out that some Canadian measures were responses to Trump's own tariffs. It also says Canada's dairy rules were agreed to in a trade deal between Canada, the United States and Mexico.

Sara Albrecht, who leads the Liberty Justice Center, said the tariffs affect not only importers but also shoppers in both countries.

Gellert says the trade fight hurts it from both sides. It pays a 50% tariff on Canadian cheese, and Canada taxes the American cheese its Canadian branch sells. One of its suppliers makes brie in Canada using milk from farms in New York, then ships the cheese back to the United States.
why_it_matters: The case could help decide how much power a president has to set tariffs on his own, which affects prices and businesses in both the U.S. and Canada.

background_read: A tariff is a tax a country charges on goods that come in from other countries, which can make those goods cost more.
The United States and Canada are close neighbors and trade huge amounts of goods, including food, with each other.
Congress has passed trade laws that give the president some power over tariffs, and courts can decide whether a president has used those powers correctly.
The U.S. Court of International Trade is a special federal court that hears cases about tariffs and trade.
